title: agno-agi/agno v3.1.2 — v3.1.2
body:
# Changelog

## New Features:

- **Conversation Compaction**: `Agent(compaction=True)` keeps long sessions inside the context window by folding older turns into a summary. Stored messages are never rewritten: a `CompactionRecord` in the new `agno_compactions` table drives a derived model payload, so removing the record restores the full conversation. Tune with `Compaction(model=..., compact_at_tokens=..., uncompacted_runs=...)`, fold on demand with `agent.compact()` / `acompact()`, and inspect `run.compaction`. With `searchable=True` the agent gets a `search_compacted_history` tool, a regex grep over the archived transcript. See [cookbook](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/blob/main/cookbook/02_agents/03_context_management/compaction/compaction.py). (#9873)
- **Codex External Agent**: Added `CodexAgent`, an adapter for OpenAI Codex built on the `openai-codex` SDK, alongside the Claude Agent SDK, LangGraph, DSPy and Antigravity adapters. Codex runs its own agent loop; the adapter translates its notifications into Agno run and tool-call events, maps each Agno session to one Codex thread (persisted when a `db` is set), and exposes `sandbox`, `approval_mode`, `reasoning_effort`, `output_schema` and MCP config. Works standalone and through AgentOS. See [cookbook](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/blob/main/cookbook/frameworks/codex/codex_basic.py). (#10901)
- **HyDE Query Transform**: Added `QueryTransformer` as a new retrieval hook and `HyDE` as its first implementation: `Knowledge(vector_db=..., query_transformer=HyDE())` searches with a hypothetical answer instead of the raw question, while rerankers still score against the original query. `HyDE` uses its own `model`, then the calling agent or team's model, then the framework default. See [cookbook](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/blob/main/cookbook/07_knowledge/02_building_blocks/12_hyde_query_transformer.py). (#10527)
- **Browser Origin Policy**: Added `AgentOS(cors=CORSConfig(origins=..., origin_regex=..., merge_base_app=...))` and opt-in `PublicSurface(enforce_browser_origins=True)`. One origin policy is now shared by CORS preflights, public run and cancel admission, auth error headers, workflow WebSockets and MCP aliases, and CORS is the outermost middleware so error responses carry consistent headers. `cors_allowed_origins` keeps its existing behaviour. See [cookbook](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/blob/main/cookbook/05_agent_os/27_public_pages/browser_origins.py). (#10869)
- **Configurable Follow-ups**: `followups: bool | FollowupConfig` on Agent and Team. `FollowupConfig` sets a count range (`num_followups` or `min_followups` / `max_followups`), a separate model and custom instructions that go only to the follow-up call. The default prompt now stays within the answer's boundaries and no longer re-offers a request the answer declined. Existing `num_followups` callers keep getting exactly N suggestions. title: agno-agi/agno v3.1.3 — v3.1.3
body:
# Changelog

## New Features:

- **Durable External Agent Sessions**: `ClaudeAgent` sessions now resume on any replica. The Claude SDK session id is stored on the Agno session (#10903), and with a database that supports transcript storage (`PostgresDb`, `AsyncPostgresDb`, `SqliteDb`, `AsyncSqliteDb`) every transcript line is mirrored into the new `agno_transcripts` table, so a later turn on another machine resumes from the database instead of a local file. A stored session that cannot be resumed falls back to a fresh SDK session seeded with the Agno history. Claude and Codex non-streaming runs now keep tool calls and results in run history. See [cookbook](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/blob/main/cookbook/frameworks/claude-agent-sdk/transcript_store.py). (#10904)
- **Background Runs & Cancellation for External Agents**: `ClaudeAgent` and `CodexAgent` support `background=True`, durable-queue run ids, resumable indexed SSE and cancellation through `/agents/{id}/runs/{run_id}/cancel`, sharing the background task, slot and event-stream infrastructure of native agents. Claude uses a per-run SDK client and Codex retains turn handles, so the owning process can interrupt either SDK. See [cookbook](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/blob/main/cookbook/frameworks/claude-agent-sdk/background_cancel.py). (#10905)
- **Step Replay for ClaudeAgent**: `ClaudeAgent.continue_run` / `acontinue_run` take the same `continue_from`, `fork` and `input` arguments as `Agent.continue_run`, with `stream=True` and `background=True`. Each tool result is a checkpoint listed by `GET /agents/{id}/runs/{run_id}/checkpoints`; continuing forks the stored SDK transcript at that message, so the model only remembers what happened up to it, and `continue_from="last_user"` replays the turn. A finished run is never rewritten in place: its continuation is a new sibling run. See [cookbook](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/blob/main/cookbook/frameworks/claude-agent-sdk/continue_from/01_continue_finished_run.py). (#10917)
- **Retries for External Agents**: `ClaudeAgent` and `CodexAgent` take `retries`, `delay_between_retries` and `exponential_backoff` with the same defaults as `Agent`. A failed attempt is retried with the same run id and resumes the SDK session or Codex thread it started; limits (`max_turns`, `max_budget_usd`, Codex budget and usage limits) and permanent errors (authentication, billing, bad requests, context window, policy) are not retried. Tool calls from failed attempts are kept exactly once, streaming consumers get a `type: "retry"` warning event between attempts, a retried run records `metadata["attempts"]`, and the durable queue fails a job at once when the agent marks its error non-retryable, including across worker restarts. See [cookbook](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/blob/main/cookbook/frameworks/claude-agent-sdk/claude_retries.py). (#10937)

title: stanfordnlp/dspy 3.4.1 — 3.4.1
body:
# DSPy 3.4.1

DSPy 3.4.1 makes GEPA's structured `InstructionProposer` the default instruction proposer and lets `dspy.RLM` build DSPy sub-agents from inside its REPL. It also adds Python 3.15 support, fixes a 3.4.0 import crash, and includes streaming, adapter, and interpreter fixes.

```bash
pip install --upgrade "dspy==3.4.1"
```

**Upgrade notices.** GEPA's default reflection request changes shape, so optimization results can differ from 3.4.0 even with the same seed. The reflection LM must now be a `dspy.LM` that can return JSON. Every RLM prompt now includes a sub-agent section, and `max_llm_calls` now also counts sub-agent LM calls. `dspy.ReActV2` signatures can no longer declare inputs named `history` or `tools`. Programs saved on 3.4.0 with a null `Score` level no longer load. See [API and Compatibility Changes](#api-and-compatibility-changes).

The [3.5 LM-interface cutoff](https://dspy.ai/community/normalized-lm-api-migration/#the-35-cutoff) announced in 3.4.0 still applies. Legacy `forward()`/`aforward()` custom LMs, the legacy-engine wrappers, custom `complete_legacy()` shortcuts, and OpenAI-style `messages=` calls are deprecated and will be removed in 3.5. `lm("hello")` stays supported.

## Highlights

### `InstructionProposer` Is GEPA's Default Proposer — @dbreunig

`dspy.GEPA` now builds `InstructionProposer()` when you don't pass `instruction_proposer=`. The old default formatted reflective examples into one raw prompt and pulled the new instruction out of backticks. The new one calls the reflection LM through `dspy.Predict` with a `JSONAdapter`. Reflective examples stay structured, so `dspy.History` inputs, tool trajectories, and `dspy.Type` values such as `dspy.Image` (including nested images) reach the reflection LM as structured content instead of text placeholders. GEPA's reflection instructions are unchanged.

You can configure the proposer directly:

```python
import dspy
from dspy.teleprompt.gepa import InstructionProposer

optimizer = dspy.GEPA(
    metric=metric,
    reflection_lm=dspy.LM("openai/gpt-5"),
    instruction_proposer=InstructionProposer(
        skills=["./skills/prompt-engineering"],
        additional_instructions="Write instructions in imperative voice.",
        max_chars=1500,
        truncate_history_outputs=True,
    ),
    auto="medium",
)
```

- `skills`: reference material for the reflection LM. Pass a path, a directory containing `SKILL.md`, an inline string, or a list of these. YAML frontmatter is parsed at construction.
- `additional_instructions`: extra guidance applied to every proposal.
- `base_instructions`: replaces the reflection prompt but keeps its input and output fields.
- `max_chars`: a hard character limit. A draft that is too long gets one compression attempt; DSPy never truncates an instruction.
- `truncate_history_outputs`: shortens long tool and REPL outputs inside history inputs before rendering, without changing the originals.

title: An Autonomous Multi-Turn Red Teaming Engine for Agentic AI Systems and MCP-Based Tools
body: This paper presents MCPRedTeam, an autonomous multi-turn red teaming engine for evaluating the security of agentic AI systems that use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for tool invocation. Unlike existing single-turn prompt injection scanners, MCPRedTeam generates multi-step adversarial strategies, executes them as realistic multi-turn conversations against live MCP-connected agents, and evaluates the resulting tool-call traces against configurable safety policies using a judge LLM. Evaluation across three benchmark agentic scenarios shows that multi-turn probing detects 3.8x more policy violations than single-turn baselines, with 74% of violations being multi-turn-dependent. The most severe findings include credential exfiltration through chained tool calls, privilege escalation across multiple turns, and safety bypasses via context poisoning. The engine is designed for authorized security testing and educational use only.

title: $τ$-Emotion-Bench: Exposing the Interaction Fragility of LLM Agents through Real-World User Emotions
body: In long-horizon tool-calling tasks, LLM agents can fail not only because of tool-use errors, but also because of ineffective interaction with users. Yet existing benchmarks largely assume cooperative and behaviorally stable users, leaving the effect of emotional variation on agent reliability underexplored. We introduce $τ$-Emotion-Bench, a ten-domain benchmark for evaluating tool-calling agents under controlled emotion-conditioned user interactions while preserving the underlying task objective. To scale both benchmark construction and agent training, we introduce Tracer, a scalable agentic data-generation pipeline that constructs grounded, policy-valid tasks and collects trajectories through an interactive agent--user--environment harness. By allowing dissatisfied users to terminate inefficient interactions, the harness provides an interaction-aware signal that filters trajectories with excessive user dependence and favors effective tool use. Experiments with two user simulators show that frontier agents remain unreliable, with substantial gaps between average task success and consistent task completion. Tracer-generated supervision consistently improves Qwen3 models across scales, generalizes to unseen domains, and transfers to $τ$-Bench and $τ$-Trait. Behavioral analyses further show that higher task success is associated with a better balance between tool execution and necessary user follow-up. Overall, $τ$-Emotion-Bench and Tracer provide a scalable framework for evaluating agent reliability under diverse user behaviors and improving tool-calling agents through interaction-aware supervision.

title: One Monitor Does Not Fit All: Formalism-Agnostic Runtime Verification for Agentic AI
body: Agentic AI systems combine model decisions, mutable state, tool calls, and delegation to external agents. Monitoring them requires observations from different execution boundaries, while prevention requires control before an operation produces its effect. We present AgenticRV, a runtime-verification architecture that separates these boundaries from the monitoring formalism. Adapters emit canonical events; each monitor receives its own projection and abstraction; and a decision policy uses normalised verdicts to select a reaction supported by the responsible adapter. We formalise when observations suffice, monitor replacement preserves decisions, and blocking prevents unsafe effects. We also distinguish rejected attempts from completed effects, avoiding the assumption that a blocked request must leave every monitor in a permanent violation state. The Python implementation supports LangGraph, MCP, and A2A. A controlled LangGraph experiment combines an external Reelay temporal monitor with a programmatic report monitor; ablations show why both are needed for the selected requirements. Differential checks and cross-adapter tests provide further integration evidence. An LLM-driven incident-response example illustrates the same enforcement path, while existing microbenchmarks isolate framework costs. The results support reuse of monitoring methods at explicit control boundaries, subject to the stated observation and deployment assumptions.

title: Unreachable Oracles: Auditing Ground-Truth Derivability in a Synthetic Tool-Drift Benchmark for LLM Agents
body: A tool-migration benchmark for LLM agents contains two objects that are easy to conflate: the behaviour under test and the oracle that scores it. This work asks whether the latter is well formed. We operationalize oracle identifiability under declared information rights at the level of the individual item: a ground-truth item is reachable only if its target value and every construction step are derivable, under a declared finite derivation grammar, from the information granted before the method's first call. We implement this criterion as a deterministic offline auditor with typed outcomes. Applied to a self-authored synthetic tool-drift benchmark, the audit finds 50 of 310 argument-pair items unreachable (16.1%), concentrated in two drift families. A separate 45-item required-field audit finds 20 additional unreachable items, reducing strict complete-call retention to zero in two families. Four derivation-grammar configurations reproduce the same 260/10/40 reachable/target-absent/convention-unobservable split. Twenty hand-adjudicated real Model Context Protocol version pairs are representable in the audit schema and none is flagged; however, 15 of the 20 depend on hand-supplied observability annotations and therefore do not constitute an independent specificity estimate. After invalid items are excluded, the retained evaluation surface is also too small to satisfy the preregistered precision and power criterion for the intended comparative study. The results argue that oracle validity should be checked before agent performance is interpreted: a benchmark should declare its information rights, audit every ground-truth target for derivability, and verify that the retained evaluation surface remains adequate for the intended comparison.

title: Beyond Corrected Actions: Training LLM Agents on Textual Critiques
body: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for multi-turn agentic tasks that require interactions with users and environments over extended sequences of actions. A common approach to improving LLM agents is to use more capable expert models to provide training supervision, either by behavior cloning the expert's trajectories or by using the expert to correct the actions in trajectories generated by the weaker student model. Across four student models from the Nemotron 3 and Gemma 4 families on the agentic domains $τ^2$-Bench Airline+Retail and WebShop, adding critiques to action-level supervision improves performance by 8% on average over action-only distillation. Additionally, CAFT checkpoints can also provide a better warm start for reinforcement learning than expert-trajectory distillation. Our results demonstrate that textual critiques can strengthen supervision for multi-turn LLM agents.

title: Tev: Scaling Long-Horizon Agentic Environments with Dense Progress Rewards
body: Long-horizon agents have drawn growing attention for their ability to work autonomously -- from hours to days -- on economically valuable tasks, a capability essential to automated discovery and recursive self-improvement (RSI). Each task is then progressively rendered from this specification into an agent-facing environment, enabling controllable complexity and a natural progress metric. Second, we turn this metric into a training recipe: via progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS), we convert progress into a dense per-step reward that improves training efficiency and makes otherwise-intractable tasks trainable. title: CLASHarness: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Conflict in Computer Use via a Controllable and Verifiable Generation Pipeline
body: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems to automate complex computer-use workflows, yet existing benchmarks mostly assume consistent, cooperative environments. In contrast, real-world collaboration rarely runs on consistent information: peer or sub-agents frequently report outdated states, issue contradictory instructions, or compete over shared permissions and files, forcing agents to check others' outputs and verify ground truth in the environment. Evaluating such conflict resolution remains challenging: manual authoring cannot scale across complex systems, while unconstrained LLM generation produces narrative drift, answer leakage, and unsatisfiable rubrics. We introduce CLASHarness (Conflict-Loaded Agent Scenario Harness), a controllable framework for generating verifiable multi-agent conflicts in computer use, with a benchmark of 600 multi-round tasks. By combining hierarchical scenario planning with an eight-step verified micro-pipeline, CLASHarness pre-commits decisive visual facts before rendering and compiles hybrid code and semantic graders directly from executed reference trajectories, guaranteeing every task is solvable by construction. Evaluating 15 frontier models on CLASHarness reveals three core bottlenecks. First, when sub-agent outputs conflict with the environment, weaker models blindly follow misleading information, whereas stronger models inspect visual evidence to verify ground truth. Second, resolving conflicts is much harder than finding them: while agents can spot inconsistencies, actively fixing system state drops task success significantly. Third, coordination protocols remain a universal bottleneck: even frontier models fail over 58% of closing actions, often forgetting to release shared locks or hand off tasks. CLASHarness provides a scalable, verifiable foundation for building reliable multi-agent systems.

title: Interlock: From Local Correctness to Task Completion in Long-Horizon Agents
body: Large language model agents increasingly undertake long-horizon tasks in complex environments characterized by fragmented evidence, partially completed states, and dependencies across resources and artifacts. Existing agents may satisfy individual requirements while failing to maintain these relationships, producing locally correct but incomplete outcomes. These failures arise because task completion depends on relationships among environmental evidence, consequential decisions, and required effects. To address this completion gap, we propose Interlock, a framework for task synthesis that represents each task as a typed completion graph. Grounding edges connect public evidence to decisions, coupling hyperedges impose joint constraints across components, and realization edges connect decisions to all required downstream effects. Interlock compiles this graph into a resettable workspace, a public request, and an evaluation rubric. A source-coverage review checks whether the original requirements survive generation, while a public-input review checks whether the rubric is supported by the materials available to the solver. An agent-as-judge inspects execution artifacts and runs verification scripts, retaining trajectories judged to satisfy all mandatory requirements. To evaluate training utility, we fine-tune two Qwen3.6 backbones on their own accepted trajectories. Across the two backbones, training improves AutomationBench task pass rates by 4.00-4.50 percentage points, JobBench weighted scores by 3.20-6.64 points, and Harvey LAB criterion pass rates by 3.89-4.16 percentage points. These results demonstrate the training utility of the synthesized experience across external task environments.

title: StateCraft: Augmenting Video World Models with Abstract-State Reasoning
body: Video world models aim to simulate complex environments with realistic appearance and dynamics. Maintaining consistency over long interactions requires tracking past actions and understanding how those actions affect the environment. Video world models can only generate partial observations of the entire world at a time. Remembering past observations alone may not be sufficient in every scenario, as they may no longer reflect the world after a sequence of actions. We introduce a paradigm that decouples a persistent, updatable abstract state from the visual state. The abstract state keeps track of the entities' changes as the world evolves, and is used to condition the visual state, which represents the current view. We propose StateCraft, a novel architecture that pairs a language model with a video diffusion model to evolve the dynamic world. We evaluate our approach on generative interfaces, which pose a substantial challenge because a single action may change parts of the state that are not currently visible. To support training and evaluation, we develop a data collection pipeline that produces informative, densely annotated trajectories at scale without human or agent supervision, together with a benchmark measuring generation quality, memory, and controllability. On this benchmark, our approach improves surpasses the state-of-the-art baselines. We demonstrate that StateCraft maintains high self-consistency and strong generation quality over long trajectories. Because the abstract state is explicit, it can be edited directly, and generation follows edits to states never observed in the data. Finally, a proof-of-concept 3D experiment, in which actions change the illumination of an unobserved room, shows that the paradigm can also be applied to spatial environments. Project page: https://insait-institute.github.io/StateCraft/.
